summary: Describes LISP-DDT, a hierarchical database that delegates authority for mapping endpoint identifiers to routing locators among DDT nodes. It is experimental.

eli5.summary: A phone book where each section points to the next, until you find the number.

subtitle: A hierarchical database that delegates authority to find endpoint-to-locator mappings.

tldr.problem: LISP separates endpoint identifiers (EIDs, stable addresses used by applications) from routing locators (RLOCs, topological addresses used for forwarding), but someone needs to maintain a database of which EID maps to which RLOC. A single centralized database does not scale.
tldr.mechanism: LISP-DDT builds a hierarchical tree of DDT nodes, each responsible for a range of EIDs. A DDT Map-Resolver queries DDT nodes iteratively, following referrals to more specific nodes, much like how DNS resolvers follow nameserver referrals.
tldr.outcome: The system distributes the authority to maintain the mapping database among many nodes and scales to Internet-wide LISP deployments. This Experimental specification may guide the design of future Standards Track mappings systems.

today: RFC 8111 is an Experimental specification published in May 2017. It has not been obsoleted or updated. LISP-DDT remains experimental and is used in limited research and trial deployments, with no widespread production deployment yet.

sections.title: The LISP Mapping Problem
sections.content:
LISP (Locator/ID Separation Protocol) splits IP addresses into two parts: Endpoint Identifiers (EIDs), which are stable names for computers that stay the same when they move, and Routing Locators (RLOCs), which are topological addresses used for forwarding across the Internet. To forward a packet to an EID, routers need to look up which RLOC leads to it.

RFC 6833 defines the interface between LISP routers and a mapping database that stores EID-to-RLOC mappings, but leaves the internal organization of the database as an open problem. A centralized database would not scale to billions of endpoints. LISP-DDT solves this by distributing the database.

The system mirrors how DNS works: it organizes mappings in a tree, delegates authority for ranges of EIDs to different DDT nodes, and lets clients follow referrals iteratively until they reach the node authoritative for a specific EID.
sections.eli5: LISP splits addresses into a stable name part and a location part. LISP-DDT is a distributed phone book that tells routers where each name maps to.

sections.title: The DDT Hierarchy
sections.content:
Every DDT database entry is indexed by an Extended EID-prefix (XEID-prefix), which combines a Database-ID, an Instance ID (for virtual networks), an Address Family Identifier, and an EID-prefix. This allows the same EID to be used in different scopes.

The root DDT node is authoritative for all possible EIDs. It delegates authority for more-specific XEID-prefixes to other DDT nodes. Each intermediate DDT node can delegate further to child nodes that know even more-specific EIDs. A DDT Map-Server is also a DDT node but accepts registration of EID-to-RLOC mappings from Egress Tunnel Routers (ETRs). A leaf DDT node points to the actual ETRs that registered the EIDs.

DDT configuration is static and hierarchical. A DDT node is configured with its authoritative XEID-prefixes and the delegations to child nodes. The tree structure mirrors how IP address space is delegated on the Internet.
sections.eli5: A tree of servers, each responsible for a range of addresses. The root server knows about everything. Each node can point to a more specific server, or to a site that registered an address.

sections.title: Sending Queries and Following Referrals
sections.content:
When a DDT Map-Resolver needs to find the RLOC for an EID, it sends an Encapsulated Map-Request (with the "DDT-originated" flag set) to a DDT node. The DDT node responds with a Map-Referral message.

A Map-Referral contains an action code describing the response type. NODE-REFERRAL means the EID matches a delegated prefix and the resolver should query the listed child nodes. MS-REFERRAL is similar but indicates the child is a Map-Server. MS-ACK means the Map-Request reached a Map-Server with registered ETRs, so the request has been forwarded to answer the query. DELEGATION-HOLE means the EID is not delegated (not a LISP destination). NOT-AUTHORITATIVE means the queried node does not have information about the EID.

The resolver follows referrals iteratively until it receives an MS-ACK, at which point it stops and waits for a Map-Reply from the ETR. The process resembles DNS resolution: follow referrals deeper into the tree until you reach an authoritative server.
sections.eli5: Send a question to a DDT node. It either answers "check this other server" or "I forwarded your question to the right place". Keep asking until you get the second answer.

sections.title: The Map-Referral Message
sections.content:
The Map-Referral message type is LISP message type 6. It carries an action code, a record of RLOCs for the referred DDT nodes, a TTL, and optional cryptographic signatures for security.

The message includes a Referral Set of RLOCs for one or more DDT nodes that are authoritative for the more-specific XEID-prefix. The resolver picks one RLOC and sends the next query to it. An Incomplete flag can be set to indicate that the Referral Set is incomplete (e.g., because not all Map-Server peers are listed), so the resolver should not cache the referral.

Each referral has an action code and a TTL. Positive referrals (NODE-REFERRAL, MS-REFERRAL) have a TTL of 1440 minutes (24 hours). Negative referrals like DELEGATION-HOLE have a TTL of 15 minutes. MS-NOT-REGISTERED has a TTL of 1 minute. NOT-AUTHORITATIVE has a TTL of 0, meaning do not cache it.
sections.eli5: The response includes addresses of servers to ask next, how long to remember this answer, and whether the list is complete.

sections.title: Securing the Database
sections.content:
LISP-DDT includes cryptographic signatures in Map-Referral messages to prevent attackers from spoofing referrals. Each referral record can carry one or more signatures. Signatures use RSA-SHA256 (RSA-SHA1 is deprecated). Each signature covers the entire Map-Referral record and includes inception and expiration times.

A DDT Map-Resolver should be preconfigured with the public keys of the root DDT node(s). When it receives a referral from another DDT node, it verifies the signature using the root's key (or keys of intermediate nodes it trusts). This prevents spoofing of entire branches of the database hierarchy.

Referral hints (shortcuts configured on DDT nodes) can create circular dependencies if used incorrectly, so clients must detect and break referral loops by tracking the prefix specificity of successive referrals.
sections.eli5: Referrals are signed with the server's private key. Resolvers verify signatures to prevent fake referrals. Clients must also detect loops where referrals keep pointing back and forth.

sections.title: Experimental Status
sections.content:
RFC 8111 is Experimental. It is published to enable research and deployment experiments with LISP-DDT and to guide future Standards Track work on LISP mapping systems. The specification is mature enough to implement but not yet part of the Internet standards.

The design enables scaling LISP to many organizations and administrative domains, each managing their own DDT nodes. It provides delegation, caching, and security mechanisms needed for a distributed EID-to-RLOC database at Internet scale.
sections.eli5: This is an experimental design. If it works well in real deployments, it may become the official standard for LISP's mapping system.
